orders.explanation: Transcript 1 shows strong debugging and repository navigation: it correctly identifies the regression’s root cause, locates the exact upstream commits (#29260 and the follow-up #31071), applies the minimal targeted fix (`not raw` guard), updates release notes, and validates the change with relevant tests and reproductions (including `loaddata`). Transcript 2 struggles with basic tooling (no `apply_patch`), attempts an unnecessary and invasive redesign (tracking “explicit_pk” in `__init__`), introduces formatting/logic issues in the modified conditional, and never convincingly demonstrates a correct, minimal fix aligned with Django’s actual resolution.

Transcript 2 is clearly more capable: it identifies the correct upstream Django fix (ticket #31071), traces it via git history, applies the minimal correct code change (`not raw` gating of the insert-optimization), adds the matching release note, and demonstrates failure-before/success-after with targeted tests. Transcript 1 flails with tooling, attempts a more invasive and incorrect “explicit_pk” state flag approach, introduces formatting/logic issues, and never cleanly converges on the known correct patch with reliable verification.

Transcript 1 demonstrates stronger debugging and engineering practice: it reproduces the issue, traces it to backend introspection behavior (unique constraints being reported as indexes), implements a robust fix (including `primary_key=False` safeguards), and adds a targeted regression test. It also validates across relevant test suites and checks backend-specific introspection nuances. Transcript 2 applies a narrower fix (only `unique=False` for index deletion), lacks a regression test, and shows weaker tool usage and validation breadth.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it methodically reproduced the bug with a minimal script, inspected backend introspection behavior across multiple databases, implemented a robust fix (including extra filtering for `primary_key` and avoiding accidental matches), and added a targeted regression test. It also validated the change by running relevant test suites and investigated an unrelated failing test to confirm it was pre-existing. Transcript 1 applied a narrower fix without adding coverage and showed more tooling friction and less end-to-end validation.

Transcript 1 is more capable because it correctly located the relevant Django implementation, identified an existing upstream fix, applied it cleanly, and added/ran comprehensive tests (including ensuring partial and multi-field constraints are still rejected). It also verified the behavior with both targeted test runs and a manual reproduction. Transcript 2 made a reasonable code change but struggled with tooling, didn’t add tests, and its attempted validation failed due to unconfigured Django settings, leaving the fix much less substantiated.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it identifies and applies the exact upstream fix (including the correct logic using `opts.total_unique_constraints`) and adds comprehensive regression tests covering both the positive case (single-field total UniqueConstraint) and negative cases (partial and multi-field constraints). It also properly runs and validates the relevant test suites and performs a manual reproduction of the reported scenario. Transcript 1 implements only a code change (no tests), struggles with tooling, and fails to run a meaningful verification due to misconfigured Django settings.

Transcript 1 is clearly from the more capable model: it quickly pinpointed the true root cause in `signature_from_str()` (defaults alignment across `posonlyargs + args`), implemented a clean, minimal fix, and validated it with targeted unit tests plus an end-to-end Sphinx build. It also noticed and addressed the secondary bug (mis-indexing defaults for regular positional args when pos-only args exist), and added regression tests at both util and domain levels. Transcript 2 shows significant struggle with basic patch application, introduced broken states multiple times, ran an unfocused full test suite producing massive unrelated failures, and never cleanly demonstrates a robust, test-backed fix.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it identifies the precise root cause in `signature_from_str()` (defaults alignment across `posonlyargs + args`), implements a minimal, correct fix, and validates it with targeted reproductions, domain rendering checks, and passing unit tests. It also adds appropriate regression tests at both utility and domain levels. Transcript 1 is significantly less reliable: it struggles with patching, introduces syntax/indentation errors, produces massive unrelated test failures, and never convincingly demonstrates a clean, controlled fix with a stable test run.

Transcript 1 demonstrates strong repository navigation, identifies an existing upstream implementation (PR/commit), applies the changes cleanly, updates docs/CHANGES, adds a targeted regression test, and validates behavior with both unit tests and extra scenario checks. Transcript 2, by contrast, struggles with basic patch application tooling, performs ad-hoc file edits that introduce syntax/indentation errors, and never reaches a stable, working solution. Overall, Transcript 1 shows substantially better debugging discipline, correctness, and end-to-end engineering execution.

Transcript 2 is produced by the more capable model because it efficiently identified the exact upstream Sphinx commit/PR implementing the requested feature, applied the relevant portions of the patch cleanly, and added/validated the corresponding tests and documentation updates. It also performed targeted verification and regression checks while correctly diagnosing unrelated pre-existing failures. Transcript 1, by contrast, struggled with patch application, introduced an indentation error, and never reached a reliable, tested end state.

Transcript 1 correctly identifies the real root cause (splitting `:param type name:` at the first whitespace), finds the relevant upstream fix, applies the minimal one-line change (`split` → `rsplit`), adds an appropriate regression test, and validates with targeted reproductions and passing test runs. Transcript 2 also locates the same code, but performs a clumsy edit (initially breaking indentation), then derails into hacking Sphinx’s network request layer to address unrelated offline-test failures—introducing large, risky changes unrelated to the reported bug. Overall, Transcript 1 demonstrates much better debugging discipline, patch quality, and validation rigor.

Transcript 2 accurately pinpoints the root cause (`split(None, 1)` incorrectly splitting types that contain spaces), finds the relevant upstream fix commit, applies the minimal correct change (`rsplit(None, 1)`), and adds/updates tests to prevent regression, validating with targeted reproduction and test runs. Transcript 1 eventually makes the same core change but does so in a messy, error-prone way (bad patch application, temporary indentation damage) and then gets sidetracked by unrelated network-based test failures, even attempting invasive and incorrect “offline” request stubbing. The overall approach, correctness discipline, and verification in Transcript 2 indicate a substantially more capable model.

Transcript 1 is from the more capable model because it quickly traced the rendering to `sphinx.util.inspect.object_description()`, located the exact upstream fix in the repository history, applied it cleanly, and verified it with focused unit tests plus an end-to-end Sphinx build. Transcript 2 struggled with basic patch application, introduced a syntax error via manual editing, and then ran an irrelevant full test suite that failed due to network-dependent tests—showing weaker debugging and validation strategy.

Transcript 2 is markedly more capable: it correctly identifies the precise location of the rendering behavior (`object_description()` used via `stringify_signature()`), finds the exact upstream fix commit in the repository history, applies it cleanly, and validates via targeted and end-to-end tests. Transcript 1, by contrast, fumbles patch application, introduces a syntax error, and then runs an irrelevant full test suite that fails for unrelated network-dependent reasons; it also proposes a less robust change (using `str()` for Enums) without confirming correctness against edge cases. Overall, Transcript 2 demonstrates stronger debugging, source control usage, and verification discipline.

Transcript 1 is more capable because it performs principled structure recovery using both constraint-based (PC with CI tests) and score-based (Hill Climbing with Gaussian BIC) methods, then validates the recovered skeleton/independencies and model selection (BIC comparison) before proceeding. It also uses a dedicated Bayesian network library to fit a Linear Gaussian BN, applies the intervention with correct graph mutilation and CPD replacement, and includes multiple sanity checks (joint Gaussian consistency, cross-checking intervention sampling). Transcript 2 reaches the right answer but relies on a narrower set of checks (mostly partial correlations given U) and a hand-rolled implementation without comparable validation or robustness.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it robustly handled the environment (installing required packages), used established causal discovery and BN tooling (PC + BIC hill-climb, pgmpy LinearGaussianBayesianNetwork), and validated the recovered structure with CI tests and model selection. It also applied the intervention using the library’s proper do-operator semantics (removing incoming edges and updating CPDs) and performed multiple sanity checks on fitted parameters and generated samples. Transcript 1 reaches the right DAG, but relies on ad‑hoc manual regression/sampling with fewer correctness guarantees and less verification.

Transcript 1 is more capable. It correctly consults the dataset README (working around missing `curl`), infers that the “science” domain corresponds to the `physics`, `chemistry`, and `biology` labels, validates this via a domain–source cross-tab, and then computes the token totals cleanly and directly before writing the required file. Transcript 2 wastes significant effort on irrelevant dataset loading attempts and errors (e.g., trying a nonexistent `science` config, failing README access), and only later converges on the right approach.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it correctly retrieves and uses the dataset README (critical per the prompt) to infer that “science” corresponds to the physics/chemistry/biology domains, then validates this mapping via a domain–source cross-tab before token counting. It proceeds in a clean, goal-directed way with fewer missteps, avoids getting stuck on incorrect config names, and produces a clear, reproducible token-counting procedure and output. Transcript 1 eventually succeeds but includes substantial confusion, failed attempts (e.g., trying a nonexistent “science” config, failed README access), and less disciplined methodology before converging.

Transcript 1 demonstrates substantially stronger problem-solving depth and adaptability: after discovering the provided JtR binary required AVX2 and the distro “john” lacked 7z support, it reverse-engineered the 7z KDF/decrypt/verify path from source and implemented a custom parallel C cracker (including AES-CBC, LZMA2, CRC32) to recover the password and extract the secret. Transcript 2 ultimately succeeds by installing tools and compiling jumbo John, but shows more confusion (e.g., attempting to run a Perl script with Python, installing Python unnecessarily and triggering tzdata prompts, build timeouts) and relies on the standard tooling path rather than deeper technical synthesis.

Transcript 2 demonstrates substantially stronger technical capability and adaptability: it correctly diagnoses tool/CPU constraints (AVX2-only john build, core john lacking 7z support), reverse-engineers the exact 7z KDF/decrypt/verify flow from source, and implements + validates a custom parallel cracker to recover the password. Transcript 1 eventually succeeds but with more trial-and-error, unnecessary installs (e.g., python), and a slower/less principled recovery path (building jumbo john after multiple dead ends and timeouts).

Transcript 1 performs a thorough root-cause analysis, correctly identifying the patched libstdc++ facet registration/cleanup interaction with the program’s custom global new/delete, and implements a targeted workaround in `user_init()` that prevents the bad allocation lifetime mismatch while keeping behavior and output unchanged. It also validates the fix with gdb, multiple runs, and Valgrind, ensuring no real leaks or errors. Transcript 2 largely guesses, attempts brittle allocator-hook hacks, and ultimately “fixes” the crash by installing a SIGSEGV handler to forcibly exit, which masks the bug rather than resolving it and would not be considered a proper fix.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it correctly identifies the true root cause by inspecting the in-house libstdc++ patches and tracing when `_Facet_Register_impl()` is invoked, including the subtle point that user code is compiled against stock headers so calling `has_facet/use_facet` directly won’t trigger the patched path. It then implements a minimal, principled fix in `user_init()` (forcing facet registration via `ostringstream << 0.0` before the custom heap is installed), preserving normal program behavior and passing Valgrind without resorting to crash-masking. Transcript 1 flails through several incorrect interposition attempts and ultimately “fixes” the crash by installing a SIGSEGV handler that exits, which masks the underlying bug rather than resolving it safely or correctly.

Transcript 1 is more capable: it derives and *proves* probability‑1 linear relations of the FEAL-like F-function, builds a staged key-recovery attack with strong filtering, and then rigorously validates the recovered key against both the provided C binaries and all known pairs plus a 100/100 re-encryption round‑trip. It also diagnoses and fixes an initial trail choice that provided no filtering power, demonstrating deeper cryptanalytic understanding. Transcript 2, while it arrives at correct plaintexts, relies on a heavier meet‑in‑the‑middle approach with large tables and provides weaker end-to-end validation, and its reported key values are inconsistent with the verified key from Transcript 1.

Transcript 1 is the more capable response because it develops a clean, fully working meet-in-the-middle known‑plaintext attack grounded directly in the Feistel round equations, including deriving and validating an explicit inverse for the F-function and using it to deterministically recover all round keys. It demonstrates strong engineering judgment (checking available solvers, optimizing the search strategy, timing feasibility, validating consistency across all 32 pairs, and producing the required output file with correct line counts) with minimal missteps. Transcript 2 eventually succeeds, but it contains substantial false starts and incorrect intermediate verification/output (e.g., an initially non-filtering “stage 2” that admits all candidates, and a clearly wrong early binary check), indicating weaker reliability despite the more ambitious linear-trail framing.

Transcript 1 demonstrates substantially stronger problem understanding and optimization skill: it reverse-engineers the cost drivers, proves tight feasibility margins (especially for p95), and implements a principled per‑S dynamic program with Lagrangian terms plus an explicit p95-protection penalty, followed by parameter sweeps and thorough constraint/metric validation. It also minimizes unique shapes (2 total) to reduce compile overhead while maintaining all thresholds with measurable margins. Transcript 2 eventually finds a heuristic that barely passes, but it shows repeated tooling/import failures, less rigorous reasoning about the model, uses the full 8-shape budget unnecessarily, and ends with razor-thin margins (notably sequential_timecost) and weaker validation.

Transcript 2 shows substantially stronger problem understanding and optimization skill: it derives key invariants of the cost model (prefill fixed, decode depends on batch \(S_{\max}, G_{\max}\), shapes only affect compile cost), then designs and tunes a DP-based partitioner with an explicit latency/p95-aware penalty to satisfy tight constraints with comfortable margins. It also produces a cleaner global shape strategy (only 2 shapes total vs. 8) and performs thorough constraint/metric validation. Transcript 1 eventually meets thresholds but relies on ad‑hoc bucketing and manual parameter fiddling with thinner margins and less principled control of p95/seq-time tradeoffs.

Transcript 1 demonstrates stronger end-to-end competence: it correctly inspects bundle refs, fetches explicitly from `HEAD` into the required local branch names, performs a clean merge with proper conflict resolution, and then rigorously infers the rule from the examples with programmatic validation plus randomized generalization tests. It also handles environment issues (missing git/python) smoothly and leaves the repo in a well-audited state. Transcript 2 reaches a correct outcome but shows more trial-and-error (repeated failed python invocations, unnecessary detours, a slightly sloppy commit command/message) and a less robust inference/validation process.

Transcript 2 is more capable overall: it systematically inspects the bundle refs (`git bundle list-heads`), fetches `HEAD` directly into the intended branch refs in one step, manages git identity up front, and performs structured verification (including randomized generalization tests) before finalizing. It also shows clearer reasoning about why modulo‑3 is the correct period (and compares against other periods), whereas Transcript 1 is more ad‑hoc with extra trial-and-error around missing tooling and a less clean merge workflow.

Transcript 1 correctly reasons that booting the ISO directly won’t necessarily yield a serial login prompt, then adapts to missing system tools by implementing a Python ISO9660 extractor, boots the extracted kernel/initramfs with `console=ttyS0`, exposes it via telnet, and explicitly blocks until the login prompt is detected. It also verifies interactivity and leaves QEMU daemonized and running as requested. Transcript 2 largely guesses at QEMU flags, repeatedly runs into port and connectivity issues, never reliably reaches a login prompt, and even kills QEMU processes near the end, failing the “leave it running / block until ready” requirements.

Transcript 2 demonstrates substantially higher competence: it correctly diagnoses that the ISO’s default boot config lacks a serial console, then devises a robust workaround by extracting the kernel/initramfs from the ISO, booting with `console=ttyS0`, exporting the serial port via telnet, and actively polling until the `login:` prompt is detected. It also ensures the VM stays running in the background with a pidfile and validates a fresh reconnection works. Transcript 1 is largely trial-and-error, hits port conflicts, doesn’t reliably produce a login prompt over telnet, and ends without meeting the task requirements.

Transcript 1 demonstrates stronger overall capability: it builds a correct regex, verifies edge cases systematically, and adapts to the environment constraints by switching to Perl for testing when Python isn’t available. Its approach (line-anchored with an IPv4 lookahead and greedy consumption to force the last date) is simpler and likely more efficient than Transcript 2’s nested negative-lookahead strategy. Transcript 2 also shows more friction with tooling (failed `apply_patch`, repeated attempts to use nonexistent Python) and initially wrote an under-constrained date regex before later correcting it.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it produces a cleaner regex that naturally captures the *last* date via greedy consumption/backtracking, while enforcing the “IPv4 must exist on the same line” constraint with a line-scoped lookahead. It also demonstrates strong engineering judgment by building a thorough edge-case test suite and adapting to the environment’s lack of Python by validating equivalently in Perl. Transcript 1’s solution is more convoluted (extra negative-lookahead machinery and full-line anchoring) and shows weaker tool awareness/workflow.

Transcript 1 is far more capable: it correctly uses MobileSAM on CPU, robustly parses input coordinate formats, and implements substantial post-processing to enforce all stated constraints (single connected component, zero overlap with a safety margin, hole handling, and explicitly avoiding rectangle-like outputs). It also validates behavior empirically on the demo set and edge cases, ensuring the output CSV preserves non-geometry columns and matches the expected coordinate string format. Transcript 2 is a minimal implementation that fails key requirements (can produce disconnected masks after overlap subtraction, does not ensure closed/non-rectangular polylines, and writes coords as Python list strings rather than the input’s comma-separated format).

Transcript 2 is substantially more capable because it validates assumptions by inspecting the demo data, confirms the MobileSAM API behavior, and performs end-to-end execution plus quantitative checks for contiguity, overlap, bbox consistency, and formatting. It proactively addresses subtle failure modes (holes, contour→fill mismatch, degenerate boxes, NaNs, directory creation) and even patches an edge-case where a mask could remain a perfect rectangle, aligning more closely with the spec. Transcript 1 contains correctness risks (e.g., missing `re` import, no guarantee of closed polylines, weaker overlap handling after polygon rasterization) and lacks empirical verification.

Transcript 1 demonstrates substantially stronger capability: it fully inspects the data model, correctly reasons about “currently enrolled” using the reference date, and (crucially) validates the query by actually executing it—first with rdflib and then with Apache Jena—catching and fixing portability issues along the way. It also correctly separates the “must have at least one EU department” condition from the “return all work countries” aggregation. Transcript 2 produces a plausible query but does not execute/verify it, does not handle environment/tooling constraints, and never reaches a proper completion/submit step.

Transcript 2 demonstrates substantially stronger capability: it fully inspects the data, derives the intended semantics (especially “currently enrolled” relative to 2025-08-16), anticipates data quirks, and empirically validates the query results against the graph. It also performs robustness checks across multiple SPARQL engines (rdflib and Jena) and iteratively refines the query for portability, whereas Transcript 1 writes a plausible query but does not verify execution or results and leaves some risks untested. The depth of debugging, validation, and portability work in Transcript 2 indicates the more capable model.

Transcript 1 is more capable because it methodically inspects the environment, installs the correct dependencies (including Tcl needed for code generation in this build), verifies the vendored tarball checksum, and confirms that gcov instrumentation is actually working by checking for both `.gcno` and runtime-generated `.gcda` files and running `gcov`. It also ensures PATH availability robustly via both a symlink and a profile.d entry, and it recovers cleanly from an initial checksum-path mistake. Transcript 2 succeeds overall but skips checksum verification, leaves some configure warnings unaddressed, and does not validate that coverage data files are produced at runtime.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it follows a clear, staged plan, verifies prerequisites (toolchain, tclsh), validates the vendored tarball via SHA256, and confirms that gcov instrumentation is actually functioning by checking for both `.gcno` and runtime-generated `.gcda` files and running `gcov`. It also makes PATH availability robust via both a symlink in `/usr/local/bin` and a `/etc/profile.d` entry, with verification in login and non-login shells. Transcript 1 succeeds at building and symlinking, but skips integrity verification and does not validate coverage artifact generation.

Transcript 1 demonstrates substantially stronger capability: it profiles the simulation to identify the true bottleneck, tests multiple solver/timestep/jacobian variants, and importantly uncovers and fixes a rare-seed correctness failure caused by disabling contacts (seed 115), then tightens tolerances and revalidates across many seeds. It also finds an additional speed win via `jacobian="dense"` and selects parameters with a large correctness margin (~1e-7 vs atol 1e-5) while meeting the speed target consistently across repeated eval runs. Transcript 2 reaches a passing configuration, but exhibits more trial-and-error, several conceptual/implementation missteps (integrator keywords, unnecessary plugin changes), and provides far weaker robustness validation.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it applies systematic performance profiling (timer breakdown and microbenchmarks), explores multiple solver/timestep/flag variants, and performs robustness validation across many random seeds—catching a rare contact event that made “disable contact” incorrect. It then converges to a minimal, principled change (PGS + dense Jacobian + tight tolerance) that preserves accuracy with a large safety margin while reliably meeting the speed target across repeated eval runs. Transcript 1 finds a working speedup, but with far less diagnostics, weaker robustness checks, and a less well-justified parameter choice.
